authors: Jeffrey Lees; Sara M. Constantino; Jean Cushen; Frederik Dahlmann; Frank G. A. de Bakker; Edoardo Della Torre; Maria Laura Frigotto; Mario Hackenbuchner; Nico Heuvinck; Emmanuel Kypraios; Anastasia Ri; Stephen Roper; Elke Schuessler; Christoph Ungemach; Dror Etzion

abstract: Climate (in)action by small business owners is not driven only by policy or economic considerations but also by sociological and psychological factors, as leaders mimic the behaviors they perceive among their peers. We find that these social inferences about what others believe are often incorrect. In this registered report of 4,432 small-to-medium business owners and leaders across seven countries, we observe a persistent gap between perceived and actual beliefs. And this gap matters: small-to-medium enterprise owners exhibiting a larger gap have fewer sustainability policies in place. These results highlight how peer effects can spur climate action among business leaders.

title: Symbolic governance and the spatial politics of disorder: Anti-social behaviour in Belfast’s ‘Holyland’
authors: Graham Ellison; Louise Rhodes
affiliations: School of Law, Queen’s University, Belfast, UK
abstract: This article examines how urban disorder is governed under conditions of contested legitimacy in a post-conflict city. Drawing on documentary analysis of institutional and policy materials from 2004 to 2025, it develops the concept of symbolic governance, defined as calibrated legitimacy management through which institutions regulate disorder while avoiding politically or reputationally risky intervention. Using Belfast’s Holyland district as an empirical site, the article traces how this logic operates across universities, policing, and local government. Revisiting social disorganisation theory, it argues that disorder is sustained not by weak social ties but by dense bonding networks within a demographically homogeneous enclave. Institutions respond through coordinated restraint and diffusion of responsibility, containing disorder within reputational thresholds while prioritising legitimacy over structural transformation.

title: Local Faces of Global Employment Practices: Media Discourses on Uberization of Labor and Institutional Adaptation
authors: Elisabeth Bethge; Mike Geppert
abstract: Uberization has become a paradigmatic case of how platform-mediated work arrangements disrupt labour markets and existing institutional structures, yet we know little about the discursive processes through which such models are reworked within divergent capitalist systems. This article investigates how Uber’s employment model is received, contested and reshaped in the United Kingdom, Germany and Mexico. Linking translation theory and Varieties of Capitalism within a discursive legitimation perspective, we examine how global platform employment practices are received, contested, and evaluated across national institutional contexts. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of 3,771 newspaper articles (2012–2023) from the three countries, combining sentiment classification with thematic analysis. We identify discursive waves of (de)legitimation around Uber’s labour practices in distinct institutional constellations. The analysis reveals three trajectories: reactive accommodation under competitive and consumer pressures in the United Kingdom as a liberal market economy; proactive regulatory resistance rooted in labour institutions in Germany as a coordinated market economy; and delayed but intense contestation in Mexico as an emerging market economy characterized by hybrid, fragmented and highly informal arrangements. The study extends the discursive legitimation perspective by linking institutional theory and industrial relations theory to show how institutionally conditioned media discourses shape the (de)legitimation of global employment practices, while bringing emerging markets and informality more centrally into Varieties of Capitalism debates.

title: Scarring the Life Course: Early Career Precarity and Long-Term Fertility Outcomes in Japan
authors: Fumiya Uchikoshi; Manting Chen
affiliations: Harvard University, USA; Southwest University of Finance and Economics, China
abstract: This study examines the long-term fertility scarring associated with nonstandard employment upon labor market entry in Japan, country characterized by dualized labor market and rigid gender norms. Analyses of retrospective occupational history data including work entry cohorts 1970–2015 with multistate life-table models indicate that early career disadvantages correlate with lower long-term fertility outcomes, especially for men. Compared to those in standard employment, men whose first job was nonstandard employment were approximately 18% points less likely to have married and 14% points less likely to have had a child by age 45. These disparities linked to nonstandard employment have increased significantly among cohorts entering the labor market after Japan’s economic downturn. Counterfactual estimates suggest that delayed or foregone marriage accounts for about one-third of the fertility penalty among men with early precarious employment. These results underscore how early labor market precarity leaves long-term demographic and social scars, especially within gender-inegalitarian contexts.

title:
When machines learn with organizations:
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
authors: Linhui Wu; Shaker A. Zahra; Niron Hashai
affiliations: Management and Organizations Department Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University Evanston Illinois USA; Strategic Management and Entrepreneurship Department Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota Minneapolis Minnesota USA; Arison School of Business Reichman University (IDC Herzliya) Herzliya Israel
abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

title: Framing the unknowable: The role of language and frame multiplicity in early‐stage startup pitches
authors: Ann‐Sophie Kowalewski
affiliations: Entrepreneurship Department IE University Madrid Spain
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations. Specifically, it considers how future growth frames interact with concreteness and novelty frames. Evidence from 618 startup pitches and ad‐hoc investor evaluations reveals that growth frames relying more on entrepreneurs' own assertions than on established grounds tend to receive lower investor evaluations. This evaluative discount is alleviated when growth is expressed concretely but becomes more pronounced when the pitch emphasizes novelty. These findings extend framing theory by explaining the relevance and possible implications of frame multiplicity in pitches and entrepreneurial communication more broadly. Managerial Summary Mobilizing support for a new venture is difficult because founders must often describe a future that does not yet exist. This study of 618 startup pitches shows that growth‐related messages can shape investor evaluations even at the earliest stage, but only if configured well. Because growth frames must appear plausible amid the uncertainty surrounding new startups, framing early‐stage startups around growth is rhetorically burdensome. Findings show that pitches are evaluated less favorably when they rely more on founders' own projections and reasoning than on established grounds such as market analyses. Concrete language can alleviate this burden, while novelty framing intensifies it. As such, this study reveals intricate and potentially unintended interactions among multiple frames within a single pitch.

title: A BOOTSTRAP SPECIFICATION TEST FOR SEMIPARAMETRIC MODELS WITH GENERATED REGRESSORS
authors: Elia Lapenta
affiliations: University of Exeter
abstract: This article provides a specification test for semiparametric models with nonparametrically generated regressors. Such regressors are not observed by the researcher but are nonparametrically identified and estimable. Applications of the test include models with endogenous regressors identified by control functions, semiparametric sample selection models, or binary games with incomplete information. The statistic is built from the residuals of the semiparametric model. A novel wild bootstrap procedure is shown to provide valid critical values. We consider nonparametric estimators with an automatic bias correction that makes the test implementable without undersmoothing. In simulations, the test exhibits good small sample performance, and an application to women’s labor force participation decisions shows its implementation in a real data context.

title: Mutualism in socio-semantic networks: structural correlates of publication output across ecosystem approaches to health
authors: Pierre Mongeau; Johanne Saint-Charles; Louis Renaud-Desjardins
abstract: Abstract While existing scientometric research has examined how individual network position and team composition affect citation-based performance, less is known about how the structural configuration of socio-semantic networks relates to collective publication output. We propose that publication output is associated with configurations that foster mutual visibility between research topics (memes) and author communities. Drawing on mutualistic network theory from ecology, we hypothesise that lower bipartite modularity (H1) and higher nestedness (H2) are associated with higher publication output. We analyse 6,406 publications across three ecosystem approaches to health (EcoHealth, One Health, Planetary Health) over 18 approach × period observations (2004–2023), linking author communities to 20 research topics identified by Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Our analyses show an empirical asymmetry: bipartite modularity is negatively and robustly associated with publication output (Spearman ρ = −0.79, p < 0.001; robust across four community detection algorithms and under leave-one-out by approach), whereas weighted nestedness shows a positive but non-significant association ( ρ = +0.39, p = 0.11), in a direction consistent with H2 but without statistical support at the cell level. The modularity result supports the H1 component of the framework: low modularity — author communities touching multiple topics — fosters mutual visibility between authors and themes. Given the observational design, we report these as field-level patterns, not causal mechanisms. The non-significant association for H2, combined with marked algorithmic variability, invites reconsidering how nestedness is operationalised in socio-semantic contexts. By integrating social and semantic dimensions within a mutualistic framework, this approach complements existing scientometric tools.

title: How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
authors: Sharjil Haque; Simon Mayer; Teng Wang
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System ,; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, ,; University of Texas at Arlington ,
abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. Our findings suggest that PE sponsors’ active engagement—through monitoring and support in distress—reduces banks’ need for monitoring and information production, enabling them to retain less skin in the game and sell loans to nonbanks.

title: Insurance and Assurance: Government Interventions and Depositor Behavior in Crisis
authors: Sümeyra Atmaca; Karolin Kirschenmann; Steven Ongena; Koen Schoors
affiliations: Ghent University , Tweekerkenstraat 2, 9000 Ghent, Belgium; University College Roosevelt , Lange Noordstraat 1, 4331 CB Middelburg, The Netherlands; ZEW Mannheim , L7,1, 68161 Mannheim, Germany; Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz , Jakob-Welder-Weg 4, 55128 Mainz, Germany; University of Zurich , Plattenstrasse 14, 8031 Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention - explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization - shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.

title: IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
authors: Christine L. Dobridge; Rebecca Lester; Andrew Whitten
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; Stanford University; U.S. Department of the Treasury
abstract: ABSTRACT Does going public affect the amount and type of corporate international tax planning? Using a panel of U.S. corporate tax return data from 2004 to 2018, we show that IPO completion is associated with the rapid implementation of multinational foreign tax structures. Specifically, within three years after filing for an IPO, firms (1) expand their presence in low-tax jurisdictions, (2) enter into cross-border agreements that accompany intangible asset transfers to foreign subsidiaries, and (3) increase the likelihood and level of foreign related-party income-shifting payments. Effects are strongest among firms with strong capital market pressure to hit post-IPO earnings targets, firms with high R&D spending pre-IPO, and firms with limited ability to use net operating loss carryforwards. We contribute to the nascent literature studying tax implications of IPOs by documenting the types and timing of specific tax strategies that enable public firms to remain lightly taxed in the post-IPO period. JEL Classifications: F23; H25; H26.

title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
authors: Leila Peyravan; Brian Rountree; Konduru Sivaramakrishnan
affiliations: Rice University
abstract: ABSTRACT Using analyst-lender affiliation in syndicated loans as a proxy for differential access to private information, we examine how unaffiliated analysts respond to this disadvantage. We find that unaffiliated analysts are more likely to herd toward affiliated analysts following loan origination, leading to improved forecast accuracy but weaker market reactions, consistent with reduced information content. In addition, herding analysts improve their forecast accuracy for other firms in their portfolios relative to nonherding analysts, suggesting a reallocation of effort. To capture information acquisition directly, we analyze IP address data from SEC EDGAR log files and find that unaffiliated analysts increase search activity, driven primarily by those not designated as herding. Although herding behavior wanes after the first year post-loan, elevated EDGAR searches persist for three years. Overall, our study provides novel evidence on how selective access to private information influences analysts’ competitive behavior. title: Structuralizing the stress process: states as contextual determinants of stress and mental health
authors: Rachel Donnelly; Zhe Zhang; Mateo P Farina; Blake W Powell
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Vanderbilt University, USA; Department of Human Development and Family Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, USA
abstract: Abstract Despite growing evidence that policy environments influence mental health, we have limited knowledge of how policy environments influence the stress processes that shape mental health. This study develops and tests a theoretical framework that structuralizes the stress process model by explicating how the state policy context (1) directly influences mental health, (2) indirectly influences mental health via stress exposure, and (3) mitigates the impact of stressors on mental health. This study uses nationally representative data from the Household Pulse Survey (2020–2023; n = 3,043,961) and the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS; 2015–2019; n = 1,989,932) merged with state policy liberalism data to consider how state policy liberalism—the ideological orientation of state policies—shapes mental health. Results show that more liberal state policies were associated with lower odds of probable depression, probable anxiety, and frequent mental distress and weakened associations between three focal economic stressors—income loss, financial hardship, employment status—and mental health outcomes. Moreover, the association between state policy liberalism and mental health was partially mediated by financial hardship. Findings differed slightly by age: mediation via financial hardship was more evident among older adults (65+), whereas the buffering of economic-related stressors was mostly among adults under sixty-five. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of a structuralized stress process model for mental health research.

title: Leaving together: social influence and church decline
authors: Elis Carlberg Larsson; Peter Hedström
affiliations: Institute for Analytical Sociology, Linköping University , 601 74 Norrköping ,
abstract: Abstract Church membership has declined across much of the Western world in recent decades. Existing research has identified individual characteristics that affect individuals’ likelihood of leaving their churches, but far less is known about how social interactions influence church decline. We examine (1) how exposure to others leaving the Church of Sweden affects individuals’ likelihood of leaving and (2) the aggregate membership dynamics generated by these micro-level processes. Using full-population register data from 2002 to 2023 and a dynamic matched-sample design, we estimate social-influence effects and assess how susceptibility varies with religious embeddedness, defined as the extent to which individuals are socially connected to other church members. We use these estimates to calibrate an agent-based simulation model linking individual behavior to aggregate membership decline. The results show that exposure to leavers increases individuals’ likelihood of leaving the Church, particularly among those with weak religious embeddedness. The simulations indicate that social influence contributed appreciably to the numerical decline of the Church of Sweden, while religious embeddedness moderated this effect. Social influence can thus amplify ongoing religious decline, while religious embeddedness attenuates this amplification.

title: Framing Democracy: How Elites' Discourse Shapes Citizens' Understandings of Democracy and Enables Backsliding
authors: Selim Erdem Aytaç
abstract: abstract: Citizens' divergent understandings of democracy have important implications for democratic resilience, yet the sources of this heterogeneity remain contested. The author argues that partisan elite discourse is a key driver of these divergent understandings: political leaders' framing of democracy systematically shapes their supporters' democratic priorities. Observational and experimental evidence from Turkey supports this argument. The author establishes that Turkish party leaders differ in how they conceptualize democracy in public discourse, and these differences map onto their supporters' understandings of democracy. A population-based survey experiment shows that when leaders emphasize particular dimensions of democracy, copartisans also assign greater importance to those same dimensions of democratic governance. These findings highlight how partisan elite framing can influence mass conceptions of democracy in ways that enable democratic backsliding: would-be autocrats can exploit this dynamic to subvert liberal norms without significant backlash, even where overall support for democracy remains high.

title: The Paradox of Imperial Taxation: How Diversity Shaped Fiscal Development in the Ottoman Empire
authors: Yusuf Magiya
abstract: abstract: This article investigates the relationship between diversity and state building by examining how diversity affects the costs of investing in fiscal capacity. The author argues that diversity—ethnic or religious—makes populations less legible to the state, thereby increasing those costs. Higher costs deter the state from investing in fiscal capacity in more diverse areas, which hinders fiscal capacity building in those regions. Instead, the state diverts investments to less diverse areas, which are typically populated by the core/dominant group. As a result, the dominant group bears a higher tax burden compared to minority groups, which do not experience comparable tax increases. The author tests these arguments using original data on local-level fiscal revenues in the late Ottoman Empire along with qualitative and quantitative evidence from archival sources and contemporary cross-national and subnational data.

title: Political Socialization In Authoritarian Regimes: Sites and Everyday Experiences for Young People in Zimbabwe
authors: Marjoke Oosterom; Simbarashe Gukurume; Tinotenda Chishiri
abstract: abstract: Scholarship on political socialization has largely overlooked how forms of violence and repression experienced by young people living in authoritarian regimes affect their political development. Bringing together the literatures on political socialization and violence, this study aims to advance debates on youth political socialization in authoritarian regimes. How and where do young people in such contexts develop political orientations and behaviors, and through which mechanisms? To address these questions, this study draws on qualitative research with urban youths in Zimbabwe between 2019 and 2022 to demonstrate the significance of everyday encounters with authoritarianism in contested urban spaces. The authors advance existing scholarship by conceptualizing and analyzing diffuse socialization experiences and sites of socialization, showing how ruling party agents operating at urban markets use diverse socialization practices to cultivate loyalty to the ruling party among young traders. The authors argue that political socialization in this context does not foster genuine loyalty but provides tacit knowledge about authoritarian politics and how to navigate it through performative compliance.

title: Renewing Democracy: How Exposure to Electoral Turnovers Reinforces Citizens' Democratic Support
authors: Damien Bol
abstract: abstract: A prevailing narrative argues that citizens who live under democratic rule take it for granted, potentially leading to democratic backsliding. This article advances a more optimistic perspective, arguing that electoral turnovers—that is, elections that displace the head of government—reinforce democratic support. To test this argument, the author merges multiple international surveys that cover more than 350,000 respondents in seventy-nine countries, matches those surveys with a century's worth of electoral data, and identifies the national electoral turnovers to which each respondent was exposed throughout their life. Cohort analysis shows that exposure to turnovers, especially those that occur after prolonged periods of incumbency, has a positive and lasting effect on democratic support. Further analysis reveals that the effect is positive in a wide range of contexts, but is strongest among citizens who have always lived in a democracy. This finding thus suggests that frequent electoral turnovers are important to renew citizens' support for democracy.

title: When Does Civil Society Prevent Violence? Civic Networks, Demography, and Communal Conflict in Côte d'Ivoire
authors: Philip A. Martin
abstract: abstract: This article explores whether local civic networks can reduce the risk of violence in communally divided societies. The author argues that dense associational networks can foster intercommunal peace near elections, but only when those networks are situated in communities diverse enough that civic networks foster intergroup contact and monitoring by local elites. Leveraging new village-level data and interviews from Côte d'Ivoire, the author examines the relationship between the country's civic associations and the political violence that occurred during national elections in 2020 and 2021. Contrary to the arguments of civil society skeptics, he shows that robust networks of voluntary associations had significant spillover benefits for peace, particularly in communally diverse areas. However, in areas with a dominant communal group, civic networks had little impact on the risk of violence. The findings inform debates about the constraints on intercommunal conflict and the significance of associationalism in divided societies.
